source_text: Quod uero non solum quaedam daemones futura praedicunt, uerum etiam quaedam mira faciunt, pro ipsa utique sui corporis excellentia, cur non contemnatur a prudentibus, cum plerique iniqui ac perditi homines ita exerceant corpora sua tantaque diuersis artibus possint, ut ea qui haec nesciunt nec aliquando uiderunt, etiam narrata ut credant? quam multa funiambuli ceterique theatrici artifices, quam multa opifices maximeque mechanici miranda fecerunt? num ideo meliores sunt bonis et sancta pietate praeditis hominibus? quae ideo commemoraui, ut qui haec sine peruicacia et sine uana resistendi animositate considerat, simul cogitet, si de subiacenti crassiore materia uel sui quisque corporis uel terrae et aquae, lapidum atque lignorum metallorumque uariorum tanta quidam homines possunt, ut eos illi, qui haec non possunt, plerumque stupendo in sui comparatione diuinos uocent, cum quidam illorum sint artibus potentiores, quidam istorum moribus meliores. quanto maiora et mirabiliora pro subtilissimi corporis, hoc est aerii facultate ac facilitate daemones possint, cum tamen sint prauitate uoluntatis maximeque superbiae fastu et inuidentiae malitia spiritus inmundi atque peruersi! quantum autem ualeat aeris elementum, quo eorum corpora praeualent, ad multa uisibilia inuisibiliter molienda, mouenda, mutanda atque uersanda longum est nunc demonstrare et puto quod uel mediocriter consideranti facile occurrat.
thought_title: Demons' wonders do not make them better than good humans
orientation: Augustine is continuing his argument that demonic abilities, whether predictions or wonders, do not make demons superior to good people.
pass_a_gloss: But truly, not only do demons predict certain future things, but they also do certain wonders, on account of the very excellence of their body; why should this not be despised by the prudent, when very many wicked and ruined men so train their bodies and are able to do so much by various arts, that those who do not know these things and have never seen them, even when they are told, can scarcely believe them? How many things have tightrope walkers and other theatrical performers done, how many things have craftsmen and especially engineers done that are wonderful? Are they for that reason better than good men and men endowed with holy piety? I have mentioned these things for this reason, so that he who considers these things without obstinacy and without a vain eagerness to resist may at the same time think, if from the underlying denser matter either of each one's own body or of earth and water, of stones and woods and various metals, certain men can do so much that those who cannot do these things, for the most part, in their amazement by comparison with themselves call them divine, although some of the former are more powerful in arts, some of the latter better in character; how much greater and more wonderful things can demons do by the capability and ease of their most subtle body, that is, their airy body, although they are nevertheless unclean and perverse spirits by the depravity of their will and especially by the arrogance of pride and the malice of envy! But how much the element of air, by which their bodies prevail, is able to accomplish, move, change, and turn about many visible things invisibly, it would be long now to demonstrate, and I think that it readily occurs even to one considering it moderately.

choices.why: Keeps the verbal force of faciunt and the noun mira as wonders, matching the contrast with predictions.

choices.term: pro ipsa utique sui corporis excellentia
choices.english: on account of the very excellence of their body
choices.why: Preserves the causal force of pro and the emphasis of ipsa and utique.
Standard English for the Latin term; keeps the theatrical context.
In this context mechanici refers to those skilled in mechanical arts and devices.
Renders praeditus as endowed and keeps sancta pietas as holy piety, matching the moral contrast.
Keeps the physical sense of subiacens and the comparative crassior as denser, contrasting with the subtle airy body.

pass_b_english: But as for the fact that demons not only predict certain future events but also do certain wonders—on account of the very excellence of their body, why should a wise person not despise this, when many wicked and depraved people so train their bodies and can do such things by various skills that those who do not know these things and have never seen them believe them even when they are merely described? How many wonders have tightrope walkers and other theatrical performers done? How many have craftsmen done, and especially engineers? Are they for that reason better than good people endowed with holy piety? I have mentioned these things so that whoever considers them without obstinacy and without a vain eagerness to resist may at the same time reflect: if from the underlying denser matter of their own bodies or of earth and water, of stones and wood and various metals, certain people can do such things that those who cannot do them often call them divine in amazement by comparison with themselves—though some of the former are more powerful in their skills, and some of the latter are better in their character—how much greater and more wonderful are the things demons can do by the capacity and ease of their most subtle body, that is, their airy body, even though they are unclean and perverse spirits in the depravity of their will, and especially in the arrogance of their pride and the malice of their envy! How much power the element of air, in which their bodies excel, has for invisibly undertaking, moving, changing, and turning many visible things would take long to demonstrate now, and I think it readily occurs to anyone who considers it even moderately.

problems.why: Source says 'so that they believe them even when told'; English inverts to 'scarcely believe'.
problems.fix: believe them even when they are merely described
problems.ruling: 'etiam narrata ut credant' means 'even when told, so as to believe'; 'scarcely believe' inverts the meaning.

edits.old: can scarcely believe them even when they are described
edits.new: believe them even when they are merely described

fixed: Changed 'can scarcely believe them' to 'believe them' because the source 'etiam narrata ut credant' means 'so that they believe them even when told', not 'scarcely believe'.

last_rejected.quote: when many wicked and depraved people so train their bodies
last_rejected.source_quote: cum plerique iniqui ac perditi homines ita exerceant corpora sua
last_rejected.why: "plerique" means "many" or "most," but "iniqui ac perditi" is "unjust and lost/damned," not "wicked and depraved"—stronger moral judgment in English than source.
last_rejected.fix: when many unjust and lost people so train their bodies
last_rejected.ruling: 'iniqui' = unjust/wicked; 'perditi' = lost/ruined/depraved. Both within normal range; not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: even when they are merely described
last_rejected.why: "narrata" means "told/narrated," but the Latin says they believe them "even when told" (not "merely described"—the point is belief despite not seeing, not diminutive "merely").
last_rejected.fix: believe them even when told of them
last_rejected.ruling: 'merely described' captures 'narrata' (told/recounted) vs. seeing; within normal range, no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: though some of the former are more powerful in their skills, and some of the latter are better in their character
last_rejected.source_quote: cum quidam illorum sint artibus potentiores, quidam istorum moribus meliores
last_rejected.why: The antecedents are confused: "illorum" = those skilled people (the ones called divine), "istorum" = those who call them divine. English reverses or obscures this contrast.
last_rejected.fix: though some of the former are more powerful in skills, some of the latter better in character
last_rejected.ruling: 'former' = skilled people (illorum), 'latter' = those who call them divine (istorum). English correctly preserves the contrast.

last_rejected.quote: even though they are unclean and perverse spirits in the depravity of their will, and especially in the arrogance of their pride and the malice of their envy
last_rejected.source_quote: cum tamen sint prauitate uoluntatis maximeque superbiae fastu et inuidentiae malitia spiritus inmundi atque peruersi
last_rejected.why: Latin has "spiritus inmundi atque perversi" as predicate nominative/apposition, not "they are unclean and perverse spirits in..."—the prepositions misstructure the Latin syntax.
last_rejected.fix: and yet they are unclean and perverse spirits in the depravity of their will, above all in the arrogance of pride and malice of envy
last_rejected.ruling: 'they are unclean and perverse spirits in the depravity...' faithfully renders 'sint...spiritus inmundi atque peruersi' with ablative phrases; no meaning lost.
